nh_summit_cliff_the_highlands.blurb: A tall schist face perched high on Rattlesnake Mountain in the northwest corner of Rumney, roughly 200 feet at its biggest. It holds 18 routes, nearly all of them bolted, plus a couple of trad lines and one top rope. Two easy 5.7 climbs aside, the grades concentrate in the 5.10s and 5.11s, with a few 5.12s and a single 5.13. Expect sustained, sometimes long lines on clean rock, while the older trad lines tend to be damp and mossy. It sees far fewer people than the main walls, largely because the steep, scrambly gully leading up to the base, with a fixed rope in the worst part, discourages visitors.

nh_yellowknife_buttress.blurb: A large schist slab high on the mountain in the northwest crags of Rumney, quiet enough that the holds often stay unchalked. The front face is close to vertical with technical, crimpy face climbing, and the gully on its right side offers slabbier lines. Of its 18 routes, most are bolted, with a few trad lines and one aid climb. A couple of easy 5.6 and 5.7 routes exist, but the bulk of the climbing is in the 5.10s and 5.11s, backed by several 5.12s and one 5.13. The wall feels shady, and some routes are long enough that a 60 m rope may not reach the ground when lowering.

nh_3_the_big_wall.blurb: The central and tallest section of Longstack Precipice, a granite cliff above Knights Pond near New Durham in the Lakes Region, with views toward Lake Winnipesaukee. Lines here run up to about 170 feet and the face is steeper than its neighbors, interrupted by roofs, ledges and short corners. The climbing is almost entirely trad, with two aid lines, and a standard rack and a 60 m rope handle most of it. Grades span 5.7 to 5.11; the 5.10s are the largest group, with a fair number of 5.8 and 5.9 options too. Expect an adventurous feel, reached by a walk of roughly twenty minutes.
nh_3_the_big_wall.approach: Follow logging roads marked with cairns from the parking area, about 20 minutes, then pick up the maintained trail along the base of the cliff.

nh_03_tier_2_boulders.blurb: A cluster of large boulders on its own level above Tier 1 within Sundown Bouldering, off the Kancamagus Highway west of Conway near the Albany Covered Bridge. The 18 problems begin with easy V0 slabs and are mostly V0 to V4, then thin out through V5 and V6 up to a lone V8. Styles are mixed: aretes, slabs, powerful compression lines and crimpy faces, including a few tall problems. Landings are flat, so you need fewer pads than at many areas. Lichen is present, so a brush is handy. It is a short 5 to 10 minute walk up from Tier 1, with a few path options.

nh_left_end_the_2.blurb: The first crag you meet when walking in along the old railbed at Dumplingtown Hill, near Candia in southern New Hampshire's Merrimack Valley. The main wall is long and low, between about 12 and 20 feet, and a big detached block on its left forms a small corridor. Most of the 18 climbs are boulder problems, plus a couple of trad lines and one top rope. Difficulty is wide: a handful of easy to moderate problems up to V4, then a hard cluster running from V7 up to V11. The hill faces the sun and dries quickly, making it a quieter alternative to Pawtuckaway. Bring pads and a spotter.

nh_tuckerman_ravine.blurb: A glacial bowl on the eastern side of Mount Washington in the Presidential Range, reached from Pinkham Notch. This is steep, serious terrain above treeline, and the climbing is ice, mixed and snow gullies rather than rock. Graded ice runs from WI1 to WI4, with frozen waterfalls and short steps, while the remaining routes are snow and alpine lines. The gullies face different directions: some catch early sun, while the northeast-facing one stays shaded and holds its snow longest. Bring an axe and crampons and know how to use them; slides, icefall and rockfall all happen in the bowl.
nh_tuckerman_ravine.approach: From the Pinkham Notch visitor center, walk the Tuckerman Ravine Trail up to Hermit Lake Shelter, which looks into the ravine; keep on the same trail to reach the bowl floor.

nh_the_g_spot.blurb: A small sport and ice spot at Rumney, spread over three lightly wooded tiers: lower, middle and upper. The bolted routes are mostly easy to moderate, mainly 5.5 to 5.9, with a couple at 5.10 and 5.11. In winter a single ice vein splits into three flows. Most are boulder-problem height or 20 to 40 feet, graded WI2 to WI4, and a couple of lines link the tiers into a multi-pitch outing of around 200 feet. Rumney's cliffs face south, so ice can melt quickly in the sun, and thin snow can leave icy rock on the traverses. Rappelling is the usual way down.
